tx.t: This morning we are going to look at some basic facts about the Moon. The Moon is about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres from the Earth.
It takes about twenty-seven days to orbit the Earth once. The same side of the Moon always faces us, because its rotation takes exactly as long as its orbit.
Gravity on the Moon is only about one-sixth of gravity on Earth. In nineteen sixty-nine, Apollo Eleven became the first mission to land humans there.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Marlow. It began in two thousand and nine with six hundred and seventy-two bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by eighty per cent, and on a busy day there were more than thirty-three thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: theft and damage. The council solved it with a tracking system fixed inside each frame.
Today, a ride costs one pounds twenty-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: In this lecture I will describe how honeybees live and why they matter so much to farmers. A single summer hive can contain up to sixty thousand bees, but only one queen.

The queen can lay as many as two thousand eggs in one day. Worker bees live for only about six weeks in summer, and they spend their lives doing different jobs, from cleaning the hive to collecting nectar.

In its whole life, one worker produces only about one-twelfth of a teaspoon of honey. Bees tell each other where food is by dancing. The angle of the dance shows the direction, and its length shows the distance.
Many crops, such as almonds and apples, depend on bees to carry pollen from flower to flower.

items.title: The history of a market town

tx.t: I would like to tell you about the history of Calder. The town received its market charter in twelve fifty-three, and it became known for its pottery.
In eighteen fifty-one, the population was about two thousand. Over the next fifty years it grew to twenty-five thousand.
Then things changed, because the main road was moved outside the centre. As a result, fewer travellers passed through the market.

tx.t: Today I will outline how solar power works and why its use is growing. Solar panels contain photovoltaic cells, which turn sunlight directly into electricity.
Most cells are made of silicon, the second most common element in the Earth's crust. The first practical silicon solar cell was made at Bell Laboratories in nineteen fifty-four.
A typical modern panel converts about twenty per cent of the sunlight that hits it into electricity. Over the last decade the cost of panels has fallen by about ninety per cent.
A panel usually works for about twenty-five years, although its output slowly declines.

tx.t: In today's lecture, I will talk about the growth of cities. In two thousand and seven, for the first time in history, more than half of the world's people lived in cities.
The United Nations expects the figure to reach about two thirds by twenty fifty. Cities take up only about two per cent of the Earth's land, but they produce most of the world's wealth.
Rapid growth can cause housing shortages, traffic jams and air pollution. Some cities are planting trees and building cycle lanes to make urban life healthier.

qs.q: When did more than half the world's people first live in cities?

tx.t: In this lecture we will look at the diversity of languages around the world. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today.
About forty per cent of them are endangered, which means they are at risk of disappearing. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, while English is the most widely spoken language overall.
Papua New Guinea is the most linguistically diverse country, with more than eight hundred languages. Just twenty-three languages account for more than half of the world's population.
A language usually disappears when children stop learning it at home.

tx.t: Researchers at Northfield College carried out a study in twenty twenty-four to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed three hundred and nine students over nine weeks.
On average, the students studied for three hours a day. However, only fifty-two per cent of them used any planned method.

The students who used the method of studying in short sessions with breaks remembered more of the material a week later. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.
